desc:
Each element [l, r] of intervals covers all integers from l to r inclusive; the intervals are unsorted and may overlap. Each query [a, b] (with a ≤ b) asks: is every integer from a to b covered by at least one interval?

The union may be built from several intervals, so a query can be covered even if no single interval contains it. For each query, in order, return 1 if it is fully covered and 0 otherwise.

intervals = [[1, 3], [4, 6], [9, 12]]
queries   = [[2, 5], [1, 6], [6, 9], [10, 11], [0, 3]]
result    = [1, 1, 0, 1, 0]

Notice that [1,3] and [4,6] do not overlap, but leave no integer in between, so [1,6] is covered. The query [6,9] fails because 7 and 8 are missing.
hints: Checking every integer of a query is far too slow for big ranges, and testing the query against each interval separately misses unions.
Build the merged blocks first. After merging, a query is covered exactly when it lies inside one single block.
Merge sorted intervals when l ≤ blockEnd + 1 (adjacent integers leave no hole). For a query, binary-search the last block starting at or before a and check that its end is at least b.
editorial: Sort the intervals by left end and merge them into disjoint blocks, joining two intervals whenever the next one starts at most one past the current end: [1,3] and [4,6] leave no integer uncovered, so they become [1,6]. After merging, there is a hole between any two blocks, so a query range is fully covered if and only if it fits entirely into a single block.

For a query [a, b], find the last block whose start is at most a with a binary search over the block starts; the query is covered exactly when that block exists and its end is at least b. Building costs O(n log n) and each query O(log n).
